title: Plant-Forward Planetary Health Diet Linked to 28 Percent Lower Heart Disease Risk in Women
excerpt: A 20-year study of more than 65,000 postmenopausal women found that even moderate adherence to the EAT-Lancet diet — rich in vegetables, whole grains and legumes — was associated with significantly reduced cardiovascular risk.
body:
• A 20-year study of over 65,000 postmenopausal women found that those most closely following the Planetary Health Diet had a 28% lower risk of overall cardiovascular disease compared to the lowest adherence group.
  • The benefits extended across specific conditions: lower risks of coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure were all observed, and even moderate adherence showed meaningful reductions.
  • The Planetary Health Diet emphasises fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts and unsaturated fats while limiting red and processed meats, added sugars and refined grains.
  • The findings were presented at NUTRITION 2026, the American Society for Nutrition's annual meeting, and align with separate studies published in JAMA Network Open and the Nutrition Journal.

Women who follow a plant-forward diet emphasising whole grains, vegetables, legumes and healthy fats may significantly reduce their risk of heart disease, according to one of the largest and longest studies to examine the Planetary Health Diet's cardiovascular effects in a postmenopausal population.

The research, presented at NUTRITION 2026 in National Harbor, Maryland, tracked more than 65,000 postmenopausal women over 20 years and found that those whose diets most closely aligned with the Planetary Health Diet had about a 28 percent lower risk of overall cardiovascular disease compared to women in the lowest adherence group. The study also found reduced risks of coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure.

Small Changes, Significant Returns

Perhaps the most practical finding: women did not need to follow the diet perfectly to see benefits. Even moderate adherence was associated with a measurably lower risk, suggesting that incremental dietary changes can make a clinically meaningful difference.

"Our results suggest that people may not need to follow a perfect or very restrictive diet to see potential heart-health benefits. This is especially important for postmenopausal women, because cardiovascular risk increases with age and tends to rise after menopause."

— Donya Shahamati, doctoral student in public health, University of California, Irvine

Lead researcher Donya Shahamati outlined simple, achievable changes: filling half the plate with vegetables more often, substituting avocado or olive oil for butter, choosing oatmeal or whole-grain cereal for breakfast, or incorporating a meatless meal once per week.

What the Planetary Health Diet Looks Like

The Planetary Health Diet was proposed by the EAT-Lancet Commission in 2019 as a framework that benefits both human health and environmental sustainability. It centres on fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts and unsaturated fats while limiting red and processed meats, added sugars, refined grains and saturated fats. Unlike rigid elimination diets, it allows flexibility — encouraging a shift in proportions rather than complete exclusion of any food group.

The diet's emphasis on plant-based proteins, whole grains and healthy fats aligns closely with traditional Indian dietary patterns that rely heavily on dal, vegetables, whole wheat and rice. For communities already eating this way, the research provides scientific validation of long-standing culinary wisdom.

Growing Evidence Across Multiple Studies

The NUTRITION 2026 findings are not isolated. A separate study published in JAMA Network Open examined 38,283 women from the Nurses' Health Study II and found that the Planetary Health Diet Index was associated with the lowest risk of incident obesity during the menopause transition, with a hazard ratio of 0.46 — meaning roughly half the obesity risk compared to low adherence.

Another study, published in the Nutrition Journal, followed 7,873 U.S. adults aged 50 and older and found that those in the highest adherence quintile had a 59 percent lower risk of all-cause mortality. Each one standard deviation increase in diet adherence was linked to a 25 percent reduction in mortality risk.

The Indian Context

India faces a growing burden of cardiovascular disease, now the leading cause of death in the country. The Planetary Health Diet's compatibility with Indian cuisine — built around lentils, seasonal vegetables, whole grains and spices — makes it particularly actionable for the diaspora and for health-conscious families in India. The research suggests that maintaining or returning to traditional plant-forward eating patterns, rather than adopting Western processed food diets, may offer protective cardiovascular benefits.

What's Next

The NUTRITION 2026 findings are based on observational data, meaning they show associations rather than definitive cause-and-effect relationships. Researchers are calling for intervention trials to test whether actively shifting women toward the Planetary Health Diet produces measurable improvements in cardiovascular outcomes. In the meantime, the accumulating evidence from multiple large cohort studies points in the same direction: a modest shift toward plant-forward eating is associated with meaningfully lower risks of heart disease, obesity and premature death — benefits that don't require perfection to achieve.
